message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
**Verdict: not ready to send.** The recommendation is clear, but the two claims it rests on, price insensitivity and a revenue floor, don't hold up as written. Decision-makers who check the numbers will find these problems.

## Must fix

**1. The June-to-July evidence doesn't show price insensitivity (Section 3).**
Your own Table 1 shows July is a peak month (harbour festival, school holidays). Occupancy rises from May to August every year regardless of price. An 81% → 89% move from June to July is what you'd expect from seasonality alone, so it can't be attributed to the £10 rise. It also covers one month and one price point, and it was a £10 rise on a £135 base, not £20 on £145.
- A fairer test compares July 2025 against July 2024, or against the competitor set's June-to-July movement.
- Add August and September, which are the real post-rise months, if they help.
- If no clean comparison exists, say so and soften "not price sensitive" to something like "no sign of a negative reaction so far".

**2. The £204,000 figure uses the wrong room count (Section 5).**
Section 2 says 112 rooms; the calculation says 124. At 112 rooms, 104 nights, 79% occupancy and £20, the figure is about **£184,000**. Either 124 is a typo and the headline falls by about £20k, or the context section is wrong. Fix this first, because it's the easiest error for a reader to catch.

**3. £204,000 isn't a floor, and the two-night minimum has an unpriced downside.**
- The estimate assumes occupancy holds at 2025 levels. That is a no-change assumption, not a conservative one. If occupancy falls, revenue falls. The "at least £204,000" wording in the recommendation should go.
- A useful framing is that revenue breaks even if weekend occupancy falls about 9.6 points (79% → ~69%). Showing that gives a more honest sense of the risk.
- Valuing the extra Friday and Sunday nights at zero is cautious, but you also put zero on the cost: single-night Saturday guests who won't book two nights. With 31 sold-out Saturdays, each lost booking is a lost full-rate night. Also, Sunday isn't a BAR weekend night, so extra Sunday nights earn the midweek rate, not £165.

**4. The two-night minimum collides with the wedding business (Section 4).**
Weddings next door account for about 38% of Saturday-night room bookings, and those guests typically arrive Saturday and leave Sunday, which is a one-night stay. The document never says whether they are exempt. If they aren't, you risk the largest single source of Saturday demand. If they are, the minimum covers far less than "Saturday nights" implies, and the benefit shrinks. The summary's "corporate and group commitments are protected" doesn't address this: Section 6 only honours *already contracted* corporate and group rates, and wedding blocks are booked through couples, possibly with future bookings not yet contracted. State the policy explicitly and quantify the exposure.

## Should fix

- **Value-for-money 8.4:** This measures satisfaction at £145, so it can't show how guests will react at £165. A high score is equally consistent with guests being near their limit. Also say where competitor scores come from, since your own survey can't have scored them.
- **Monitoring trigger:** "Review the rate" is vague. Say who decides, by what date, and what the options are (roll back, discount, exempt certain dates). Also note that bookings already on the books at £145 will mask early pick-up, so the first month's data will look better than the underlying trend.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023":** No data is given. Add it or cut it.
- **Competitor comparison:** The £20 to £35 gap is only meaningful if the three hotels are truly comparable. Also say whether any of them run minimum stays.
- **Dates:** The document is dated April 2026 and proposes a 1 June 2026 start, with a 15 May load date. If it's going out now, those dates have passed and need updating.

## Summary for the author
The idea may well be sound, but "well-evidenced, low-risk" overstates it. Your one natural experiment is confounded by seasonality, the headline number has an internal inconsistency, and the wedding exposure is unaddressed. Fixing those three, and reframing £204k (or £184k) as a central estimate with a stated break-even, would make this much harder to pick apart.
